newsitem.title: UK: All interruptible gas users in southern Britain cut.
newsitem.headline: All interruptible gas users in southern Britain cut.

text.p: All interruptible gas contract holders in the southern half of Britain have been interrupted for the gas day starting at 0600 GMT on Thursday, a spokesman for British Gas Plc's transport and distribution arm TransCo said.

Roger Griffiths, commercial manager within TransCo's commercial operations department at Hinckley in Leicestershire, said that all available interruptions in the southern half of the country were called late on Wednesday for the current gas day.
The gas day runs for 24 hours from 0600 GMT. TransCo will keep the situation under review, he added, and will decide later on Thursday if interruptions will also apply on Friday.

Interruptible gas contracts are held by large gas users and are cheaper than "firm" contracts, which guarantee delivery. Interruptible contract holders are expected to have alternative fuel sources, such as fuel oil, available so they can continue operations if TransCo needs to interrupt their gas to ensure continued supply to other users.

The National Transmission System, the pipeline network operated by TransCo, is designed to cope with two extremes. The first is a single day when demand reaches a level expected only once every 20 years. And the second is a prolonged cold spell when demand reaches a level only seen once every 50 years.
Griffiths said that demand for Thursday is expected to reach 80 to 90 percent of a once-in-every-twenty years peak day, or approximately 360 million cubic feet.

He added that the cold snap across Britain this winter is more difficult for TransCo to deal with than last year's cold weather, as the cold is mostly concentrated in the south, where the higher population density inevitably means demand is higher. Last winter the coldest weather occurred in Scotland.
The largest single entry point for gas from the North Sea is St Fergus in Scotland, so it has further to travel to reach the demand centres.

Griffiths said there is a possibility that demand will rise further next week, when industry and business are fully functioning again after the Christmas break. But he added that the main incremental demand now is from domestic consumers, and demand next week will depend entirely on the weather.
TransCo is already using gas from storage to meet the extra demand, he said.
